# Summary

We conducted multilevel meta-analyses on the two key constructs in Flynn & Lake (Bohns) (2008): estimated percentage agreement and expected discomfort of rejecting request (see Table 1 in the manuscript).  We conducted the analyses in R (R Core Team, 2017), the R package metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010), and the R package metaforest (Van Lissa, 2020).  We also followed recommendations by Harrer and colleagues (2021). 
For each construct, we constructed both a three-level, full model where we nested individual effect sizes of scenarios (in Experiment 1a) or conditions (in Experiment 4) in studies to account for potential between-study heterogeneity, as well as a two-level, reduced model where the between-study heterogeneity was set to zero, which is equal to fitting a simple random-effects model in which all effect sizes are assumed to be independent.  Despite that effect sizes are nested in studies, comparing the full model and the reduced model indicated that the full model did not provide a significantly better fit for either the analysis on estimated percentage agreement (*p* = .10) or discomfort rejecting request (*p* = .20).  Therefore, Table 1 reported results from the reduced models.

**References:**

* Harrer, M., Cuijpers, P., Furukawa, T.A., & Ebert, D.D. (2021). Doing Meta-Analysis with R: A Hands-On Guide. Boca Raton, FL and London: Chapmann & Hall/CRC Press. ISBN 978-0-367-61007-4.
* R Core Team (2017). R: A language and environment for statistical computing. Vienna, Austria: R Foundation for Statistical Computing. Retrieved from https://www.R- project.org/. 
* Van Lissa, C. J. (2020). Small sample meta-analyses: Exploring heterogeneity using MetaForest. In R. Van De Schoot & M. Miočević (Eds.), Small Sample Size Solutions (Open Access): A Guide for Applied Researchers and Practitioners. CRC Press. 
* Viechtbauer, W. (2010). Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. Journal of statistical software, 36(3), 1-48.



```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(metafor)
library(metaforest)

setwd("/Users/xuanzhao/Dropbox/Research-Booth/Nick Epley/Project 2 happy to help/Meta analysis/")
data_folder <- "/Users/xuanzhao/Dropbox/Research-Booth/Nick Epley/Project 2 happy to help/Meta analysis/"
file_discomfort <- "discomfort_meta.csv"
file_agree <- "perentage_agree_meta.csv"

discomfort_data <- read_csv(paste0(data_folder,file_discomfort))
agree_data <- read_csv(paste0(data_folder,file_agree))


```

# Discomfort of rejecting requests

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

#Calculate Cohen's d variance for between-subjects design

discomfort_data_b <- discomfort_data %>%
  filter(design == "Between")
  
discomfort_data_b$vi <- ((discomfort_data_b$n_requester+discomfort_data_b$n_helper)/(discomfort_data_b$n_requester*discomfort_data_b$n_helper)) + (discomfort_data_b$d^2/(2*(discomfort_data_b$n_requester+discomfort_data_b$n_helper)))

#Calculate Cohen's d variance for within-subject design

discomfort_data_w <- discomfort_data %>%
  filter(design == "Within")

discomfort_data_w$vi <- (2 * (1 - discomfort_data_w$cor)/discomfort_data_w$n_requester) + (discomfort_data_w$d^2/(2*discomfort_data_w$n_requester))

discomfort_data_new <- rbind(discomfort_data_b, discomfort_data_w)

```


## Without moderator 

### Full model

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

model.discomfort.full <- rma.mv(d, 
                  vi, 
                  slab = study_id, 
                  random = ~ 1 | study_id/es.id, 
                  test = "t", 
                  method = "REML", 
                  data = discomfort_data_new) 
summary(model.discomfort.full)

```


### Reduced model

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

model.discomfort.reduced <- rma.mv(d, 
                  vi, 
                  slab = study_id, 
                  random = ~ 1 | study_id/es.id, 
                  test = "t", 
                  method = "REML", 
                  data = discomfort_data_new,  
                  sigma2 =  c(0, NA))

summary(model.discomfort.reduced)

```

Comparing models:

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

anova(model.discomfort.full, model.discomfort.reduced)

```

## With moderator

Imagined vs. Actual as the moderator. However, the moderation effect isn't significant.

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

model.2 <- rma.mv(d, 
                  vi, 
                  slab = study_id, 
                  mods = ~ interaction,
                  random = ~ 1 | study_id/es.id, 
                  test = "t", 
                  method = "REML", 
                  data = discomfort_data_new) 
summary(model.2)

```

# Percentage Agreement

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

agree_data$vi <- ((agree_data$n_requester+agree_data$n_helper)/(agree_data$n_requester*agree_data$n_helper)) + (agree_data$d^2/(2*(agree_data$n_requester+agree_data$n_helper)))

```

### Full model

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

model.agree.full <- rma.mv(d, 
                  vi, 
                  slab = study_id, 
                  random = ~ 1 | study_id/es.id, 
                  test = "t", 
                  method = "REML", 
                  data = agree_data) 
summary(model.agree.full)

```

### Reduced model

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

model.agree.reduced <- rma.mv(d, 
                  vi, 
                  slab = study_id, 
                  random = ~ 1 | study_id/es.id, 
                  test = "t", 
                  method = "REML", 
                  data = agree_data,  
                  sigma2 =  c(0, NA))

summary(model.agree.reduced)

```

Comparing models:

```{r, echo=FALSE, message= FALSE, warning= FALSE}

anova(model.agree.full, model.agree.reduced)

```

We see that the full (three-level) model, compared to the reduced one with two levels, does not show a better fit. Therefore, given that "a two-level model provides a fit comparable to a three-level model, Occam’s razor should be applied: we favor the two-level model over the three-level model, since it is less complex, but explains our data just as well." (source: https://bookdown.org/MathiasHarrer/Doing_Meta_Analysis_in_R/multilevel-ma.html)"
